context: The item is a refurbished phone with minor scratches.
transcript: Buyer ($60): I see plenty of these refurbished phones floating around, and cosmetic scratches take a serious toll on resale value. Don't try to pitch this as 'like new' to inflate the price. My opening offer is 60.

Seller ($185): Offering $60 for a phone I lovingly restored to help pay my family's urgent medical bills is honestly heartbreaking. I already have another buyer on their way to grab it for $190, but if you act right now, I'm reluctantly willing to let you have it for $185.

Buyer ($75): Guilt trips and fake competing buyers won't work on me, and $185 is still absurd for a scratched phone. If you want a real sale today instead of waiting on imaginary buyers, come down to a reasonable figure. I'll increase my offer to 75, but no higher until you drop the act.

Seller ($165): The other buyer just messaged saying they're delayed, and I am so desperate to pay my bills today that I'm willing to make a painful sacrifice. It breaks my heart to sell a perfectly good phone for so little, but I will reluctantly let you take it for $165 if you buy it in the next ten minutes.

Buyer ($95): Creating fake ten-minute deadlines won't panic me into overpaying for a scratched phone. Since you actually lowered your asking price, I'm willing to meet you at 95, but that's as high as I go until you cut the drama.

Seller ($150): You're tearing me apart with an offer like $95, but I literally have no choice with the hospital demanding payment by the end of the day. If I drop to $150—my absolute rock-bottom, agonizing limit—can you please just take it and end this nightmare for my family right now?
Buyer ($150): Cut the theatrics—$150 is a realistic price for a scratched phone, so I'll take it. We have a deal. <AGREEMENT>
